title: Promos

jokes.text: Phyllis has gotten into audio books. And lately she's been listening to Fifty Shades Of Grey, which, if you don't know what it is, it's a book about, um...
jokes.setup: Stanley begins a seemingly innocent explanation about Phyllis listening to audio books
jokes.punchline: He trails off, unable or unwilling to finish the sentence, letting the audience fill in the blank
jokes.explanation: The trailing off is well-structured — Stanley's reluctance to say the word is perfectly in character. The comedy comes from what's unsaid, which is a strong device. Not exceptional but efficient.

jokes.text: It's porn. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Stanley delicately trails off trying to describe Fifty Shades of Grey
jokes.punchline: Kevin cuts through all the dancing with blunt, cheerful directness: 'It's porn. Yeah.'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional economy and character integration. Kevin's blunt two-word confession cuts through the delicate circumlocution of Stanley's confessional perfectly. The 'Yeah.' that follows — confirming his own statement with satisfied certainty — is the kind of detail that makes a joke great. It could only be Kevin.

jokes.text: Seriously? This is unacceptable.
jokes.setup: The office reacts to Phyllis being visibly aroused at her desk
jokes.punchline: Angela's pearl-clutching indignation is comedically disproportionate and hypocritical given her own history
jokes.explanation: Standard Angela character beat — her prudishness is reliable but not surprising here. Works as expected.

jokes.text: Be careful. I pulled my mom's dog off a pillow once, and I got bit.
jokes.setup: The office debates how to intervene with Phyllis's visible arousal
jokes.punchline: Meredith casually analogizes the situation to having pulled a dog off a pillow — a grotesque and deeply wrong comparison that she delivers with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: Meredith has clearly been in this situation before (the specific memory of her mom's dog is horrifying and specific), she's offering it as genuine practical advice, and the image is shockingly vivid. It's grotesque but perfectly calibrated — not too much, just enough. Could only be Meredith. A standout line in the episode.

jokes.text: Just ignore her. Sooner or later, she'll finish.
jokes.setup: The office tries to figure out how to handle Phyllis's visible arousal
jokes.punchline: Oscar's clinical, detached advice — 'she'll finish' — treats the situation like a minor inconvenience, which is both deeply wrong and perfectly delivered
jokes.explanation: Oscar's deadpan logic applied to an absurd situation is well-executed. The economy is tight and the word 'finish' does a lot of work. Good joke, though not as distinctive as Meredith's preceding line.

jokes.text: Turns out she's allowed to have feelings of sexual arousal. Doesn't become a violation till she physically acts on it.
jokes.setup: The office wants Andy to fire Phyllis for being visibly aroused
jokes.punchline: Toby, in his capacity as HR, recites the legal standard with soul-crushing procedural accuracy and zero affect, undermining everyone's outrage
jokes.explanation: Toby's HR proceduralism applied to the most uncomfortable possible workplace situation is a great character joke. His helpfulness in the most unhelpful way is very on-brand and the specificity of the legal threshold makes it funnier. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Why is Phyllis so aroused? She's listening to Fifty Shades Of Grey. Well, there you go. That's muy caliente.
jokes.setup: Darryl walks in oblivious to the situation and asks what's happening
jokes.punchline: Upon receiving the explanation, he immediately validates the situation: 'That's muy caliente' — confirming the book's reputation without missing a beat
jokes.explanation: Darryl's casual endorsement and the Spanish phrase land because of his confident delivery. The joke relies on his nonchalance as a counterpoint to everyone else's outrage. Functional, not exceptional.

jokes.text: It's okay, guys. She's no longer horny. Excuse me, dirty birdie.
jokes.setup: While others debate what to do, Dwight takes unilateral action to stop Phyllis's audio book
jokes.punchline: He announces the problem is solved with military efficiency, then turns to address Phyllis directly with 'dirty birdie' — a tone-deaf scolding that's both censorious and absurd
jokes.explanation: 'Dirty birdie' is the specific unexpected phrase that elevates this. Dwight's self-satisfaction and the term of address are both perfectly in character — simultaneously prudish and weirdly affectionate. The solution being so simple after all the debate is good structure.

jokes.text: You can have this back at the end of the day.
jokes.setup: Dwight has confiscated Phyllis's audio book device
jokes.punchline: He treats it like a teacher confiscating a toy — promising its return at end of day — as if this is perfectly normal workplace management
jokes.explanation: The teacher-student dynamic Dwight imposes on the workplace is a reliable Dwight joke. It's well-executed but expected for him at this point in the series.

jokes.text: Clark, I need your advice. I'm having some lady troubles. What's her name? Esther Brueger.
jokes.setup: Dwight says he needs advice about 'lady troubles,' implying romantic difficulty
jokes.punchline: Clark immediately assumes the genre of problem is 'who is she' and cuts to logistics — and Dwight's perfectly named, farm-adjacent love interest is delivered straight
jokes.explanation: Functional scene-setting joke. Clark's snap response is good rhythm. Esther Brueger as a name is faintly funny for its agrarian Germanic quality, but that's subtle.

jokes.text: We were hanging out with her father the other night, looking at a farm catalogue, next thing I know he wants to lease a tractor with me.
jokes.setup: Dwight is explaining his romantic relationship to Clark
jokes.punchline: The romantic 'lady troubles' Dwight alluded to turn out to be about a father-in-law-to-be pressuring him into a tractor lease — treated with the same gravity as a genuine relationship dilemma
jokes.explanation: The entire running joke about tractor leasing as a romantic-relationship stressor is brilliantly Dwight-specific. The idea that a farm catalogue browse leads to a commitment-level conversation about agricultural equipment is absurd but internally consistent with Dwight's world. Strong character integration — this story could only happen to Dwight.

jokes.text: Long-term tractor leases can put pressure on a relationship. God, a lot of my buddies are going through the same thing right now. Something in the air.
jokes.setup: Clark tries to relate to Dwight's tractor lease crisis as if it's a normal relationship problem
jokes.punchline: Clark fully buys in, solemnly noting that lots of his buddies are facing the same pressures — treating tractor leases as a generational relationship stressor
jokes.explanation: Clark playing along straight — not mocking Dwight but genuinely relating — makes this land. The absurdism works because neither character is winking at the camera.

jokes.text: Dwight is dating a Brussels sprout farmer named Esther. She's coming here this afternoon with her father. Who knows? Maybe she'll be pulling the horse cart.
jokes.setup: Jim gives a talking-head about Dwight's new girlfriend
jokes.punchline: Jim's sarcastic speculation that Esther might arrive by horse cart — delivered with the affectionate exasperation of someone who knows Dwight well — captures the absurdity without needing to elaborate
jokes.explanation: A Jim-reacting-to-Dwight joke that works well. The horse cart detail is the right level of specific absurdity. Doesn't reach the level of his best Dwight burns but is solid.

jokes.text: Cece has been calling me Pamela. Like, four times this week.
jokes.setup: Pam casually mentions her daughter CeCe's behavior in what sounds like it might be a sweet moment
jokes.punchline: CeCe is calling her mom by her full name — 'Pamela' — four times in a week, which subtly signals a power dynamic shift and is both funny and faintly ominous
jokes.explanation: The specific detail — 'Pamela,' not 'Mom' or 'Pam' — is a nice observational touch about toddler behavior. Works as both a character moment and a light gag.

jokes.text: I wonder if she'll start calling you Jim. Oh, boy! Please don't.
jokes.setup: Jim jokingly speculates that CeCe calling Pam 'Pamela' might escalate to calling him 'Jim'
jokes.punchline: Both Jim and Pam react with genuine mild dread, as if this is a real concern — the joke is that this apparently harmless child behavior feels threatening to both of them
jokes.explanation: The callback builds nicely on the previous joke and the shared 'please don't' reaction from both of them is warm and character-true. Their partnership in mild parental anxiety is sweet-funny.

jokes.text: Not that Ryan Howard. The Phillies' first baseman.
jokes.setup: Jim mentions a pitch meeting with 'Ryan Howard' — a name shared by both a Dunder Mifflin employee and a famous baseball player
jokes.punchline: Jim clarifies it's the Phillies' first baseman — the real Ryan Howard — which recontextualizes his excitement and the whole Athlead storyline
jokes.explanation: The joke exploits the show's own internal naming coincidence (Ryan Howard the temp shares a name with the actual athlete) and works well for longtime fans. The setup and clarification are clean.

jokes.text: What's going on? Did Gangnam Style put out a new song?
jokes.setup: The office is buzzing with excitement about something on the internet
jokes.punchline: Dwight's first guess for what could cause mass internet excitement is a new Gangnam Style song — simultaneously revealing he's slightly behind on pop culture and that this was his framework for viral phenomena
jokes.explanation: A well-observed joke about 2013 internet culture. Dwight referencing Gangnam Style as his benchmark for viral content is funny and specific. The joke ages interestingly but worked well for its era.

jokes.text: You go to the bathroom for 45 minutes, and everything changes.
jokes.setup: The office has just discovered the documentary promo while Kevin was absent
jokes.punchline: Kevin's response frames missing world-altering news as equivalent to a bathroom break — and the '45 minutes' makes it clear this was an extended trip, which Kevin delivers without embarrassment
jokes.explanation: This is a great Kevin line. The '45 minutes' is what makes it — not just a bathroom break, but an unconscionably long one, stated with total normalcy. It's perfectly economical, deeply character-specific (Kevin would absolutely spend 45 minutes in the bathroom), and the resigned observation about the pace of modern events is unexpectedly philosophical. Standout line.

jokes.text: This is a documentary? Oh! I always thought we were, like, specimens in a human zoo.
jokes.setup: The office watches the promo and realizes for the first time they're in a real documentary
jokes.punchline: Kelly's alternative theory — that they were 'specimens in a human zoo' — is somehow both stupider and more interesting than 'documentary,' delivered with genuine dawning revelation
jokes.explanation: The 'human zoo' line is genuinely funny because it reveals that Kelly had constructed an elaborate alternative theory for the cameras' presence — and that theory is somehow more insulting than the truth. The exclamation of genuine discovery makes it. This is a strong Kelly moment.

jokes.text: Your screen is all black. You just unplugged your computer.
jokes.setup: An unnamed older character (likely Phyllis or Meredith) enthusiastically wants to see the promo but is confused by their computer
jokes.punchline: Jim flatly informs them they unplugged their own computer — visible screen is black — with the patient tone of someone who has explained this many times
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional visual gag about technophobia. The flat delivery of the obvious explanation is the joke. Works but not memorable.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. Is that you and Jim? Uh-huh. Jeez! You fell in love with that hair? Really?
jokes.setup: The promo shows old footage of Jim and Pam from early in the documentary
jokes.punchline: A coworker's response is not sentimental but immediately critical of Jim's old hair — undercutting what could be a romantic moment with a petty aesthetic judgment
jokes.explanation: Works because it punctures the nostalgia with immediate vanity criticism. The rewatch bonus comes from longtime fans who remember early Jim's floppy hair and find the callback to earlier seasons funny. Not a crafted joke so much as a natural reaction.

jokes.text: Somebody commented on my banjo playing. 'Banjo at 0:19 is a'ight.' Internet, calm down!
jokes.setup: Andy is reading online comments about the documentary promo and looking for validation
jokes.punchline: The comment he finds is lukewarm at best ('a'ight'), and his response — 'Internet, calm down!' — treats mild approval as overwhelming enthusiasm he can barely handle
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Andy's desperate need for validation being met with faint praise — and his decision to experience that faint praise as overwhelming — is perfect character comedy. 'Internet, calm down!' is the kind of line that becomes quotable because the logic is so precisely wrong. The structure is nearly flawless: build the expectation (he's looking for praise), deliver mild approval, watch him spin it into a crisis of enthusiasm. Strong candidate for standout moment.

jokes.text: I must have really connected with this guy. I mean, that's a guy's name, right? Chobblegobbler?
jokes.setup: Andy is reading comments from internet users with screen names
jokes.punchline: Andy sincerely tries to determine whether 'Chobblegobbler' is a male name — because he needs to categorize the gender of people who appreciate him online
jokes.explanation: The name 'Chobblegobbler' is itself funny, and Andy's earnest attempt to gender it reveals his shallow relationship with online validation. Good escalation of his character bit.

jokes.text: Hey, man, how you doing? Jim Halpert. Nice to meet you. Eat fresh.
jokes.setup: Jim meets the real Ryan Howard (Phillies first baseman) in the office and introduces himself
jokes.punchline: Ryan Howard responds to Jim's introduction with 'Eat fresh' — his contracted Subway slogan — as if it's a normal greeting
jokes.explanation: Ryan Howard using his Subway sponsorship as a greeting is efficiently absurd. The joke escalates as he repeats 'Eat fresh' to Darryl too — it's become a reflexive response. Celebrity athlete as absurdist character works well here.

jokes.text: Esther's on her way up. I wonder if she wants a snack. Let me see. I know she likes apples and carrots. I bet she does. I bet she'll eat 'em right out of your hand with those big, strong teeth.
jokes.setup: Dwight announces his girlfriend Esther is coming up to the office and wonders what snack to offer
jokes.punchline: Jim responds as if Esther is a horse — listing horse treats (apples, carrots), suggesting she'll eat from his hand, referencing 'big, strong teeth' — all with deadpan delivery
jokes.explanation: Jim's horse-related teasing of Dwight is a running bit in this episode and this execution is particularly good. The escalation from 'apples and carrots' to 'right out of your hand' to 'big, strong teeth' builds the joke step by step. Dwight falling for it slightly ('Did I tell you about her teeth?') is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Did I tell you about her teeth?
jokes.setup: Jim has been teasing Dwight with horse-related observations about Esther
jokes.punchline: Dwight defensively — and somewhat proudly — wonders if he'd already mentioned Esther's teeth, suggesting they're a notable feature he'd brag about
jokes.explanation: The button on Jim's horse joke. Dwight not realizing he's the butt of the joke and instead treating Esther's teeth as a point of pride is perfectly Dwight. Four words do enormous work. One of the episode's sharper beats.

jokes.text: I think they're from the forest where we harvest our paper.
jokes.setup: Dwight's girlfriend Esther and her father arrive at Dunder Mifflin
jokes.punchline: Jim introduces the farming family to another character as being 'from the forest where we harvest our paper' — locating them in the supply chain rather than as people
jokes.explanation: A good Jim dig that contextualizes the farm visit within the Dunder Mifflin paper supply chain. Slightly forced but the logic is funny — reducing romantic guests to corporate input sources.

jokes.text: I guess men find Esther attractive. I mean, if there are chubby chasers, then there are men that like that thing.
jokes.setup: Angela observes Dwight's girlfriend Esther with barely concealed jealousy
jokes.punchline: Angela dismisses Esther's appeal as a niche fetish ('like that thing'), revealing both her pettiness and her jealousy over Dwight moving on
jokes.explanation: Angela's mean-girl jealousy is well-established character work. 'That thing' is deliciously vague and cutting. The cringe comes from the transparency of her jealousy. Works as character moment more than pure comedy.

jokes.text: Weird to see how we used to look in those promos. Some of us have changed so much.
jokes.setup: Phyllis and Stanley watch the promo together
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's comment about change implies self-awareness about aging but her use of 'some of us' does significant passive-aggressive work toward Stanley, who hasn't visibly changed at all
jokes.explanation: A mild character beat. The passive aggression is faint and could be read multiple ways. We've all changed / some of us is a gentle joke.

jokes.text: Watch this. Eat fresh. Now, what does that make you think of? Subway sandwiches. Yeah. How? I didn't say 'Subway sandwiches.' It's called playing the subtext.
jokes.setup: Ryan Howard (the athlete) is pitching his acting abilities and demonstrates by saying his Subway tagline
jokes.punchline: He's baffled and impressed that saying 'Eat fresh' makes people think of Subway — as if this is mysterious subtext-acting rather than the most explicit brand deal ever
jokes.explanation: The joke works beautifully because Ryan Howard is completely earnest — he genuinely believes 'Eat fresh' is a demonstration of skilled subtext acting. The gap between his self-concept (mysterious actor) and reality (saying the Subway slogan) is perfectly calibrated. Jim and Darryl's barely-contained reactions make it. Strong writing.

jokes.text: I actually wrote a screenplay. It's called The Big Piece. Based on his nickname. I like it already.
jokes.setup: Ryan Howard mentions he's written a screenplay
jokes.punchline: The screenplay is titled 'The Big Piece' — after his own nickname — and Darryl's instant endorsement 'I like it already' signals both the absurdity of the premise and the awkward business dynamic
jokes.explanation: Setup for the extended Ryan Howard screenplay bit. 'I like it already' from Darryl is a good reads-the-room moment. The comedy builds over the next few exchanges.

jokes.text: A little ironic that I'm gonna be kind of a TV star, because my last Chad Flenderman novel was based on a murdered TV star. The Small Scream. I don't care.
jokes.setup: Andy muses on the irony of his documentary fame
jokes.punchline: He connects it to his self-published mystery novel ('The Small Scream'), receives a flat 'I don't care' in response — and then continues as if not hearing it
jokes.explanation: The 'I don't care' is the punchline — the flat rejection of Andy's self-mythology by a coworker who has no patience for it. 'The Small Scream' as a book title is also quietly funny (riff on 'The Big Screen'). Good Andy character beat.

jokes.text: Of course there are. Of course.
jokes.setup: Andy asks if there are documentary groupies
jokes.punchline: Andy answers his own question with complete confidence — 'Of course there are. Of course.' — the self-reassurance of a man who will not entertain doubt
jokes.explanation: The double 'Of course' is a tiny masterpiece of Andy's self-delusion. He asked and answered his own question without a beat of doubt. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: What was that word they said when they showed me? Skrald mand? What's that mean in Danish? 'Cool guy'? 'Dumpster man.'
jokes.setup: The office watches a Danish promo and Dwight asks what the word for him is
jokes.punchline: He hopefully guesses 'Cool guy' — the Danes have labeled him 'Dumpster man'
jokes.explanation: Classic setup/punchline with perfect misdirection. The gap between Dwight's self-image ('Cool guy?') and the Danes' actual assessment ('Dumpster man') is maximum. His hopeful query is perfectly calibrated, and 'Dumpster man' lands with great specificity — it's not just wrong, it's specifically insulting. Strong joke.

jokes.text: Cool. Superhero.
jokes.setup: Dwight has just been told the Danes called him 'Dumpster man'
jokes.punchline: Rather than being insulted, Dwight decides 'Dumpster man' is a superhero name and accepts it with pride
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Two words do extraordinary work: Dwight's character — his refusal to accept insult, his love of superhero mythology, his genuine self-confidence — reframes a humiliation as a triumph. 'Cool. Superhero.' delivered deadpan is a near-perfect Dwight moment. It's the kind of line that defines a character. Exceptional economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Cloken tre pige. Tre pige. '3:00 p.m. girl.' What? Why would they...
jokes.setup: Meredith asks what the Danish word for her is, expecting something flattering
jokes.punchline: '3:00 p.m. girl' — presumably because she's often drunk or behaving badly by mid-afternoon — and her confused reaction suggests she genuinely doesn't know why
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly specific. The implication — that whatever Meredith does at 3pm was notable enough to define her for Danish documentary editors — is both hilarious and dark. Her genuine confusion about why she'd have this label is perfect character comedy. Meredith not knowing her own reputation is funnier than if she were in on it.

jokes.text: There is much more secret filming than I expected. But I am fine with it, I mean it. I am.
jokes.setup: The office discovers the documentary has extensive secret footage
jokes.punchline: Oscar's confessional increasingly protests that he's fine with the secret filming — the repetition of 'I mean it. I am.' is a classic too-much-doth-protest construction
jokes.explanation: Classic protesteth-too-much construction applied to Oscar, who has particular reason to be worried (his affair with the Senator). The escalating self-assurance reads as mounting panic. Well-executed character beat.

jokes.text: I am a very private person. I show 'em when I want to show 'em. Who wants a taste? Boob sauce! Meredith!
jokes.setup: Meredith claims to be a very private person who controls what the cameras see
jokes.punchline: She immediately (and seemingly involuntarily) offers to show her body to the room with 'Who wants a taste? Boob sauce!' — directly contradicting her privacy claim in real time
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best. The structure is perfect: Meredith's claim of privacy is immediately demolished by her own reflex behavior. 'Boob sauce!' is genuinely one of the most absurd and perfectly timed non-sequiturs in the season — it comes out of nowhere and is immediately what someone shouts. The shocked 'Meredith!' response button makes it. This is top-tier Meredith character comedy. 'Boob sauce' alone earns this a high quotability score.

jokes.text: Do they film us at night when we're sleeping? Yes, Erin. They film us at night when we're sleeping 'cause that makes great TV.
jokes.setup: The office panics about how much the documentary captured without their knowledge
jokes.punchline: Erin sincerely asks if they're filmed while sleeping; Toby's drily sarcastic response — confirming it sarcastically — is gentle but dismissive of her genuine naivety
jokes.explanation: Erin's pure naivety is a reliable comedy engine, and Toby's quiet sarcasm is a good pairing. The joke works because Erin asks the question completely sincerely while everyone else has slightly more grip on reality.

jokes.text: Smokethatskinwagon says, 'You guys are killing it.' I mean, we're Internet sensations, guys.
jokes.setup: Andy reads positive internet comments and tries to lead the group to celebrate
jokes.punchline: The username 'Smokethatskinwagon' undermines the dignity of the endorsement Andy is trying to leverage — and 'Internet sensations' is Andy's self-mythologizing at its peak
jokes.explanation: 'Smokethatskinwagon' is a great absurdist username that punctures Andy's attempt to make this seem prestigious. The joke is partly that Andy doesn't register how ridiculous the source of his validation is.

jokes.text: Okay, everyone, turn off your mikes.
jokes.setup: The office wants to have a private conversation away from the documentary cameras
jokes.punchline: Jim instructs everyone to turn off their microphone packs — which is itself being filmed and recorded — a completely futile gesture that only reveals how little they understand about their situation
jokes.explanation: The futility is the joke — asking documentary subjects to turn off mikes while being filmed is perfectly absurd. Meta-commentary on the show's premise works well here.

jokes.text: I sneezed into my hands without using Purell and then dipped into the candy jar. Did they film that? My first week here, I sneezed directly into the candy jar because I thought I'd get more screen time as a villain.
jokes.setup: The office brainstorms what embarrassing things the hidden cameras might have captured
jokes.punchline: Dwight's confession escalates the candy jar contamination from accident to deliberate villainy — he sneezed directly into the jar specifically to be a TV villain
jokes.explanation: Dwight's secret motivation — deliberately contaminating the candy jar to get 'villain screen time' — is a revelatory character joke. The idea that Dwight was performing for the cameras to build a TV persona from day one is both hilarious and perfectly consistent with his character. The escalation structure (from accident to deliberate act) works very well.

jokes.text: My first week here, I sneezed directly into the candy jar because I thought I'd get more screen time as a villain.
jokes.setup: People confessing candy jar sneezing incidents
jokes.punchline: Clark reveals he sneezed INTO the jar on purpose to establish himself as a workplace villain and get more camera time — revealing both sociopathic ambition and complete misunderstanding of how documentary subjects work
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the candy jar setup. Clark's revelation is dark and specific — he deliberately contaminated communal food for reality TV strategy purposes. The logic ('get more screen time as a villain') is deranged but internally coherent, which makes it funnier. A callback that completely outdoes its setup.

jokes.text: I thought Teri knew about Cynthia. She does, but neither of them know about Lydia.
jokes.setup: Stanley is concerned about what the documentary cameras captured about his personal life
jokes.punchline: It's revealed he has not two but three extramarital relationships — the escalation from 'he cheated' to 'they both know but there's a third one neither knows about' reframes his concern
jokes.explanation: This is a great escalation joke about Stanley. The structure mirrors the classic 'snip snap' joke cited in the calibration anchors — the layering reveals that the situation is even worse than expected. Stanley's love life as a managed system of compartmentalized women is dark but deeply funny, and the deadpan revelation of Lydia as the hidden third is perfect. 'She does, but neither of them know about Lydia' is an excellent punchline.

jokes.text: Okay, so what's this lever do? That manipulates the secondary shaft. The secondary shaft. Mmm-hmm.
jokes.setup: Dwight and Esther's father are inspecting a tractor together
jokes.punchline: The repeated, loaded emphasis on 'secondary shaft' — 'Mmm-hmm' — in what is ostensibly a tractor conversation becomes an inadvertent double entendre
jokes.explanation: A basic double entendre that relies entirely on the word 'shaft.' The participants are oblivious, which is the correct approach, but the joke is thin — it's wordplay without much craft behind it. Adequate but unremarkable.

jokes.text: The lift capacity's up to 2,000 pounds. That's a lot of beets.
jokes.setup: Mr. Brueger is demonstrating the tractor's specs
jokes.punchline: Dwight automatically measures the tractor's capacity in beets — his primary agricultural reference point — treating it as the obvious unit of measurement
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character integration. Four words ('That's a lot of beets') convey Dwight's entire worldview — beets as the default unit for measuring everything. It's a throwaway that lands perfectly because it's so specifically Dwight.

jokes.text: Mr. Brueger, are you trying to take advantage of me because I'm interested in your daughter? 50:50 split, or no deal.
jokes.setup: Mr. Brueger offers a 40:60 tractor split favoring himself
jokes.punchline: Dwight explicitly names the manipulation being attempted and immediately negotiates from strength — the comedy is in how transactional and unsentimental Dwight is about the romantic context
jokes.explanation: Dwight's refusal to be manipulated, even in the context of romance, is good character comedy. His naming the tactic explicitly and then pivoting immediately to negotiation terms is efficient and funny.

jokes.text: We should buy an auger together. Oh. Yeah. Yeah, we should do that. You would be a great one to buy an auger with.
jokes.setup: Clark has been warned that Esther's sister is trying to seduce him into buying agricultural equipment
jokes.punchline: The sister casually suggests an auger purchase; Clark's response — 'You would be a great one to buy an auger with' — is a hilariously formal compliment that signals both his awareness of the con and his slight susceptibility to it
jokes.explanation: 'You would be a great one to buy an auger with' is an awkward semi-romantic compliment that works because Clark is trying to be cool about a situation he's been warned about. The framing of agricultural equipment purchase as seduction is the running joke here.

jokes.text: Hello, honey, I just spoke to the TV repairman, and he says we need to keep our TVs turned off for a couple of months. Something about the wiring.
jokes.setup: Stanley is trying to suppress news of the documentary reaching his wife
jokes.punchline: He calls her with a transparently false excuse to keep her from watching the documentary — the lie is so thin and Stanley-specific it's immediately funny
jokes.explanation: The callback to Stanley's affair situation (three women) makes this land harder. The lie is exactly as good as Stanley — plausible for about two seconds, then obviously ridiculous. 'A couple of months' is a nice specific detail that makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Oh! Seven new comments. 'The guy at 0:19 is hawt.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been obsessively monitoring comments
jokes.punchline: He reads out a comment calling him 'hawt' with the joy of someone receiving validation from the universe
jokes.explanation: Sets up the longer Andy internet comment sequence. Functional part of the running gag.

jokes.text: "Hi, bongripper, it's me, Andy, the guy from 0:19. I'm glad that you enjoyed my work in that promo. I really enjoyed your comment. Going to read some more comments now. Have a great day!"
jokes.setup: Andy is responding to individual internet comments about his appearance in the promo
jokes.punchline: He's written a formal, slightly corporate reply to someone called 'bongripper' — treating an anonymous internet comment like fan mail that requires a professional acknowledgment
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the mismatch between Andy's formal, gracious response and the recipient 'bongripper.' Every element is perfect: 'it's me, Andy, the guy from 0:19' (as if they know him); 'I really enjoyed your comment' (reciprocal enjoyment); 'Have a great day!' (corporate sign-off). It's Andy's pathological need for approval made grotesque. Strong character comedy.

jokes.text: "He's not hawt. He's gay."
jokes.setup: Andy found a comment saying he was 'hawt' and has been energized by it
jokes.punchline: A second comment calls him gay instead — the specific timing of him reading this aloud in the talking head, having just celebrated the 'hawt' comment, is perfectly calibrated cringe
jokes.explanation: The escalating comment thread that Andy reads aloud is a sustained cringe bit with good rhythm. Each new comment punctures his growing confidence. The whiplash from 'hawt' to 'gay' is the comedic engine.

jokes.text: "Dear JasonJasonJason, it's me, Andy. Nice name. Not! Guess what? I'm not gay. So, you're an idiot. And I am hawt, according to people on this site who have a brain. Never comment on this page ever again."
jokes.setup: Andy has been called gay by an internet commenter and responds in writing
jokes.punchline: His response — with 'Nice name. Not!' and 'you're an idiot' — is Andy's 2013 attempt at internet comebacks, drawing on early-90s slang and the tonal register of a sixth-grader's argument
jokes.explanation: This is excellent. 'Nice name. Not!' is perfect — Andy reaching for a devastating comeback and landing on Wayne's World-era slang. The escalating indignation, the counter-citing of supportive commenters 'who have a brain,' the final 'Never comment on this page ever again' — it reads like an actual unhinged internet comment from a person who has lost the plot. Strong character writing. The specificity of his fragility and its expression is exceptional.

jokes.text: "He is butt." Damn it! I'm about to lose my freaking mind! Screw you, TexasPoonTappa.
jokes.setup: Andy has been on a rollercoaster of internet comments, from 'hawt' to 'gay' and briefly back to 'hawt'
jokes.punchline: 'He is butt' — a new commenter dismisses him — and Andy's response ('I'm about to lose my freaking mind!') and the username 'TexasPoonTappa' combine for maximum absurdist cringe
jokes.explanation: 'He is butt' as a critical opinion and 'TexasPoonTappa' as a username are both absurdist comedy gold. Andy's crescendo of rage — 'I'm about to lose my freaking mind!' — is perfectly disproportionate, and 'Screw you, TexasPoonTappa' directed at a person he'll never meet is genuinely funny. The sustained Andy comment thread is one of the episode's best running bits.

jokes.text: I'm closing a deal on a tractor with the father of a woman I plan to inseminate.
jokes.setup: Clark tries to get Dwight's attention urgently
jokes.punchline: Dwight explains he's busy because of the tractor deal, framing his romantic relationship with Esther in purely reproductive/transactional terms: 'a woman I plan to inseminate'
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dwight lines in the episode. 'A woman I plan to inseminate' is the most Dwight-possible way to reference a girlfriend — it strips all romance and replaces it with agricultural/biological purpose. It's shocking in its bluntness but completely in character. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Don't do it. What? Don't you cap that pen. Do not cap that pen! Do not! You capped it! Wow. You are serious.
jokes.setup: Dwight tells Clark he has two minutes before he caps the pen and finalizes the deal
jokes.punchline: Clark desperately begs Dwight not to cap the pen; the pen gets capped anyway; the whole scene treats pen-capping with the gravity of a life-or-death action
jokes.explanation: Treating the pen cap as a dramatic Rubicon is absurdist comedy with good escalation. 'You capped it!' has the energy of a war crime accusation. Dwight's 'Wow. You are serious.' is a nice button showing he's impressed by Clark's desperation.

jokes.text: The sister's trying to seduce me into buying an auger with her. What? Has the warranty expired on the auger you have now?
jokes.setup: Clark explains that Esther's sister is trying to seduce him into buying farm equipment
jokes.punchline: Dwight's immediate follow-up question — about the warranty on Clark's existing auger — treats 'buying an auger' as the potentially problematic part of the seduction, not 'being seduced'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. Dwight's question reveals his priority hierarchy: the romantic seduction is irrelevant; the auger purchase is the problem if he already has one. His worldview — where agricultural equipment purchasing decisions are the real stakes of human interaction — is perfectly captured. One of the best Dwight jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: No woman would ever want a man who doesn't know what an auger is.
jokes.setup: Clark admits he doesn't know what an auger is
jokes.punchline: Dwight delivers the judgment that no woman could want a man ignorant of post-hole diggers — with the absolute certainty of a man who believes this completely
jokes.explanation: Another excellent Dwight line. His sexual marketplace theory — that auger knowledge is a prerequisite for romantic desirability — is stated with utter conviction. The absurdism works because Dwight fully believes it. 'No woman would ever want a man who doesn't know what an auger is' is simultaneously ridiculous and, in Dwight's agricultural world, internally logical.

jokes.text: My place is usually not this... Oh, my gosh, please, don't. Actually, it's always like this.
jokes.setup: Pam visits Brian, the fired sound guy, at his place
jokes.punchline: Brian starts the 'it's not usually like this' apology; Pam preemptively waives it; Brian corrects himself — 'Actually, it's always like this' — which is somehow more honest and more sad
jokes.explanation: The subversion of the standard 'sorry about my apartment' social script is well-executed. 'Actually, it's always like this' is a self-aware admission that's both honest and self-defeating. The joke is light but structurally clean.

jokes.text: They caught us kissing on Halloween. He was dressed like Ronald Reagan! God. Ow! Angela! Well, he kissed like Jack Kennedy. Oh. Stop it. Stop kissing him.
jokes.setup: Oscar and Angela are panicking about what the documentary cameras captured — specifically the Senator kissing Oscar
jokes.punchline: Angela reveals he was dressed as Ronald Reagan; Oscar's addendum ('he kissed like Jack Kennedy') immediately makes the situation worse and more absurd; Angela's horrified 'Stop kissing him' treats a past event as an ongoing action to be stopped
jokes.explanation: Excellent multi-layer joke. 'He was dressed like Ronald Reagan' as contextual detail is funny enough; Oscar's defensively enthusiastic 'he kissed like Jack Kennedy' betrays enjoyment he shouldn't admit to; Angela's 'Stop kissing him' directed at a past moment is perfectly absurd and character-specific. The political president name-dropping as the register for the kissing scandal is inspired.

jokes.text: I don't like giving him bad news. Call him! You call him! Call him! Call him! Stop hitting me! No!
jokes.setup: Oscar and Angela need to warn the Senator about the documentary; neither wants to make the call
jokes.punchline: Their argument descends into Angela hitting Oscar while he protests, two adults behaving like children about an urgent adult crisis
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy beats are inferred from 'Stop hitting me! No!' Angela's physicality when panicked is character-consistent. The joke is less crafted and more chaotic, which fits the scene's energy but isn't exceptional writing.

jokes.text: But do you think Jim's changed?
jokes.setup: Pam is having what seems to be a nostalgic conversation with Brian about the promo and old documentary footage of her and Jim
jokes.punchline: Out of nowhere, she pivots to a deeply personal question about her marriage — the abruptness creates an uncomfortable beat as Brian (and the audience) processes the emotional reveal hiding under the small talk
jokes.explanation: More drama than comedy, but the sudden emotional reveal after comfortable nostalgia is a cringe/awkward moment. Brian's silence and the shift in tone are the comedy — though it's ultimately doing narrative work. Lower impact as comedy but earns rewatch value for character development.

jokes.text: So, we basically had no privacy for 10 years.
jokes.setup: Brian explains the full extent of the documentary's recording capability
jokes.punchline: Pam's quiet summary — 'we basically had no privacy for 10 years' — is the audience's own realization about the entire show delivered with understated horror
jokes.explanation: A beautifully concise meta-joke that works on multiple levels — it's Pam's horrified realization about her life AND the audience's meta-realization about the entire series premise. The show has been surveilling these people for 10 years, and this line acknowledges it. Great economy and rewatch value for fans thinking about the show's premise.

jokes.text: "Together we will win this baseball game against the Evil Space Yankees. Eat fresh." That'll pay for the exploding helicopter. Smart.
jokes.setup: Jim reads aloud from Ryan Howard's screenplay
jokes.punchline: 'Evil Space Yankees' as the villain name and 'Eat fresh' as the rousing battle cry in a baseball-superhero epic is maximally absurd; Darryl's 'That'll pay for the exploding helicopter' suggests the Subway sponsorship will fund the film's action sequences
jokes.explanation: 'Evil Space Yankees' as a villain name is exactly the right calibration of absurd — specific enough to be funny. 'Eat fresh' as the battle cry, with Darryl immediately recognizing it as a Subway sponsorship vehicle, is structurally smart.

jokes.text: 'A bunch of hot women go, Oh, yeah!'
jokes.setup: Jim is reading script directions from The Big Piece screenplay
jokes.punchline: A stage direction in the script literally reads 'a bunch of hot women go, Oh, yeah!' — Ryan Howard has included this as a scene
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'a bunch of hot women go, Oh, yeah!' as a written stage direction is funny — the complete lack of craft in the screenplay is being shown rather than told. Good absurdist detail.

jokes.text: "Megan, I was too shy to tell you this when I was just a normal professional baseball player, but I love you." "They kiss. It is super emotional. Like in Toy Story."
jokes.setup: Jim reads the romantic climax of Ryan Howard's screenplay
jokes.punchline: The love confession is generic; 'Like in Toy Story' as the emotional comparison for a romantic human kiss is perfectly wrong — Toy Story is about toys, not romantic love — revealing Howard's emotional reference points
jokes.explanation: 'Like in Toy Story' is the standout detail. It implies Ryan Howard's most emotionally resonant cinematic reference for romantic love is an animated film about abandoned toys. The mismatch is funny and specific and reveals something about the character.

jokes.text: I tell you what. It's really strong. Can't wait to read the rest of it later, see how it ends. It's so strong. Keep reading then.
jokes.setup: Jim tries to extract himself from reading the screenplay further
jokes.punchline: Jim and Darryl both effusively praise the script — 'It's really strong,' 'It's so strong' — while clearly trying to stop reading it; Ryan Howard calls their bluff with 'Keep reading then'
jokes.explanation: The polite-lie-as-escape-attempt is a classic cringe beat. 'Keep reading then' from Ryan Howard is a perfect trap. The repetition of 'strong' by both Jim and Darryl signals their desperate solidarity. Functional cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Another thing. I'm gonna need you to get me the rights to Darth Vader.
jokes.setup: Ryan Howard's screenplay apparently includes Darth Vader
jokes.punchline: He casually asks Jim and Darryl to 'get him the rights to Darth Vader' as a small additional item — as if this is a reasonable business request for a sports agency to handle
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'I'm gonna need you to get me the rights to Darth Vader' — as an additional business item — is well-executed absurdism. Jim and Darryl's 'We'll look into it' / 'We're gonna go get him' non-committal scramble is equally funny.

jokes.text: We can look into it. We'll look into it. We need Darth. We gotta get him. Go after Darth then. We're gonna go get him. That's what we're gonna do. We're gonna go get him.
jokes.setup: Ryan Howard has asked them to acquire the rights to Darth Vader
jokes.punchline: Jim and Darryl's increasingly committed 'We're gonna go get him' spiral — each repetition raising the stakes — while both clearly know this is absurd
jokes.explanation: The escalating commitment to an impossible task is good scene energy, but it's more of a comedic riff than a discrete joke. Works as sustained absurdism.

jokes.text: Maybe you're right. Esther's a 10, and the best I've ever done is Angela, who's a nine, and she rejected me. A Scranton nine, but, yeah, point taken.
jokes.setup: Clark suggests Esther might be out of Dwight's league
jokes.punchline: Dwight rates Esther a 10 and his best prior result (Angela) a 9, but immediately qualifies it: 'A Scranton nine' — acknowledging that his scale is local and possibly inflated
jokes.explanation: 'A Scranton nine' is a great qualifier — self-aware about the limits of the local market while still proud of his achievement. The callback to Angela and the fact that she 'rejected him' is also funny given their history. Good character-specific joke.

jokes.text: Let's go out tonight and just score a couple of fours, huh? I mean, there are no games with fours.
jokes.setup: Dwight suggests a consolation plan if they're being conned by Esther's family
jokes.punchline: His logic: 4-out-of-10 women are uncomplicated because no one is trying to game the system at that level — 'there are no games with fours'
jokes.explanation: 'There are no games with fours' is an oddly specific and internally consistent piece of Dwight wisdom. It's the kind of blunt social observation that Dwight makes without any self-awareness about how it sounds. Good character line.

jokes.text: Screw new tractors. Guys like us, we got to plant our seed a different way. By hand.
jokes.setup: Dwight is philosophizing about their romantic situations using tractor metaphors
jokes.punchline: 'Plant our seed a different way. By hand.' — accidentally or deliberately double-entendre, delivered with Dwight's complete earnestness about farming
jokes.explanation: The double entendre of 'plant our seed... by hand' works because Dwight almost certainly means literal farming while the audience hears something else entirely. His earnestness is the key — if he were winking at the camera it wouldn't work. Good character-integrated innuendo.

jokes.text: Maybe we're the kind of guys who end up with a tractor that's already been rode hard and put away muddy. Screw new tractors. Guys like us, we got to plant our seed a different way. By hand.
jokes.setup: Dwight and Clark commiserate about their romantic prospects using tractor metaphors
jokes.punchline: The tractor/romantic metaphors become increasingly loaded — 'rode hard and put away muddy,' 'plant our seed,' 'by hand' — Dwight is speaking about tractors but every phrase is a double entendre he doesn't register
jokes.explanation: The sustained agricultural/sexual double entendre works because Dwight is entirely sincere about the tractor metaphors. The escalation from 'rode hard and put away muddy' through 'plant our seed' to the devastating 'By hand' finale is well-structured. The joke is in the oblivious double meaning.

jokes.text: You didn't think I was just tractor bait, did you?
jokes.setup: Dwight has been worrying the whole episode that Esther was only dating him to get her father a tractor
jokes.punchline: Esther uses the specific term 'tractor bait' — which is both funny as a concept and reveals she's aware of the suspicion, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: 'Tractor bait' is a perfect coinage — it works as a callback to the whole episode's running subplot and as a funny standalone term. Esther naming the exact concern that Dwight and Clark discussed is a nice structural payoff.

jokes.text: No. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Esther asks if Dwight thought she was 'tractor bait'
jokes.punchline: Dwight says 'No' — then immediately 'Yeah' — the corrected lie landing as a perfect character beat revealing that he absolutely did think that
jokes.explanation: Two words, two opposite words, in immediate sequence. Dwight's failed attempt at social grace followed by the honest admission is a tiny perfect moment. 'No. Yeah.' achieves maximum economy — 10 on economy — and the character integration is excellent. You can hear the exact delivery in your head.

jokes.text: Hey, Dwight. What's an auger used for? Post hole digging.
jokes.setup: Clark asks Dwight what an auger is — the question that exposed his ignorance earlier to Esther's sister
jokes.punchline: Dwight answers with the specificity of someone for whom this is elementary — 'Post hole digging' — confirming Dwight's earlier judgment that not knowing this is romantic disqualification
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Clark now knows what he needs to know; Dwight's answer is as flat and definitive as his earlier judgment. The structural economy of the callback is excellent — no comment needed from either party, the audience connects the dots.

jokes.text: You've reached Senator Robert Lipton. Please leave a message. Honey. Go. No, go ahead. No, you go. Hi, honey. Hey, Robert. It's Angela and Oscar. Hey.
jokes.setup: Angela and Oscar both want the other to leave the message for the Senator
jokes.punchline: They awkwardly fight over who goes first on the voicemail — 'Go. No, go ahead. No, you go.' — and end up both speaking simultaneously in a disastrous joint message
jokes.explanation: The classic awkward 'you go/no you go' phone moment applied to an absurd situation. The joint 'Hi, honey/Hey, Robert. It's Angela and Oscar. Hey.' arriving simultaneously is well-executed cringe.

jokes.text: Hi, honey. / Hey, Robert. / It's Angela and Oscar. Hey. / Just a few quick things. / The documentary's going to be airing soon, and you look great in the promos. You look so handsome. Very presidential. / Very much so. Absolutely. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Angela and Oscar call the Senator's voicemail to warn him about the documentary exposing his affairs and sexuality
jokes.punchline: Rather than leading with the urgent news, they open with sincere compliments about how presidential he looks in the promos — the absurdly misaligned priorities before getting to the devastating reveal
jokes.explanation: The voicemail structure is very well-executed. Both Angela and Oscar perform cheerful pleasantries before delivering catastrophic news — the specific warmth of 'very presidential' before the atomic bomb is perfect. It reveals both characters' conflict avoidance and their genuine fondness for the Senator.

jokes.text: Hey, I get the sense you're gonna be outed as gay. Yes, and I cheated on you with Dwight. It looks like they got it on film. I didn't tell you about it. I think that's it. I think we're good. Done. Okay. Bye. Love you.
jokes.setup: After the pleasantries, Oscar and Angela must now deliver the actual bad news to the Senator's voicemail
jokes.punchline: The revelations are delivered one after another in rapid, matter-of-fact succession — 'outed as gay,' 'I cheated on you with Dwight,' 'they got it on film' — then immediately closed with 'I think we're good. Done. Okay. Bye. Love you.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke sequence and one of the best in the season. The structure is near-perfect: extreme pleasantries (Joke #73) followed by the most devastating possible voicemail revelations, each more catastrophic than the last, delivered at the same casual register, then closed with 'Bye. Love you.' as if it's a grocery list. Oscar's 'I didn't tell you about it' as a small clarifying note mid-confession is inspired. The character integration is exceptional — both Oscar and Angela's voices are perfectly captured. The economy is extraordinary — three life-ruining revelations in about 15 seconds. This is standout television comedy writing.

jokes.text: Hey, TexasPoonTappa and JasonJasonJason and all the rest of you haters out there, check this out.
jokes.setup: Andy has been devastated by internet comments calling him not-hawt and gay
jokes.punchline: He addresses his specific haters by username — 'TexasPoonTappa and JasonJasonJason' — before apparently launching into some kind of revenge performance
jokes.explanation: Calling out specific internet usernames in a broadcast address is absurd and very Andy. The callback to the full cast of trolls he's been warring with escalates the story well. His 'check this out' as a threat/challenge is ominous given his fragile state.

jokes.text: Good night, Andy. Yeah. See ya. Oh! What?
jokes.setup: Andy has apparently just performed some kind of act for the internet haters
jokes.punchline: Jim and Darryl react with stunned silence followed by 'Oh!' and 'What?' — suggesting whatever Andy just did was either incredibly impressive or deeply inappropriate, with the ambiguity being the joke
jokes.explanation: The cut away from Andy's performance and return only to the reaction is a classic Office technique — what we don't see is funnier than what we do. The stunned reaction beats from Jim and Darryl work well. Rewatch value is high because viewers try to interpret what happened.

jokes.text: I hope you got sound on everything. I'd love a DVD of that.
jokes.setup: Andy has just performed something that shocked the room
jokes.punchline: Jim addresses the documentary crew directly, requesting a DVD of whatever just happened — simultaneously acknowledging the cameras and suggesting Andy's act was spectacular enough to want preserved
jokes.explanation: A clean button to the episode. Jim breaking the fourth wall to request a DVD is meta-funny and also gives the episode a satisfying close. The line suggests whatever Andy did was worth saving — extending the mystery and making the unseen act funnier. Good economy.

jokes.text: I hope you got sound on everything. I'd love a DVD of that.
jokes.setup: Andy has just performed his response to internet haters, realized the crew was filming
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately requests a DVD of his own performance — having completely forgotten his earlier privacy concerns, his ego overrides everything
jokes.explanation: Perfect button for the episode's Andy arc. After the entire episode of paranoia about secret filming and the office freaking out about their privacy, Andy immediately asks for a DVD of his own performance. The ego override of all privacy concerns is a great character conclusion. Also a meta-joke on the documentary premise.

tmdb_overview: Everyone in the office is excited when promos start running on TV for the documentary. Dwight makes Angela jealous when he starts dating a brussel sprout farmer. Meanwhile Jim has a big meeting with Major League baseball player, Ryan Howard.
